facts.text: The dollarbird is a roller named for the pale blue or white, coin-shaped spots on its wings.
facts.quote: so named because of the distinctive pale blue or white, coin-shaped spots on its wings

facts.text: It ranges from Australia to Korea, Japan and India.
facts.quote: It can be found from Australia to Korea, Japan and India.

facts.text: It is dark brown washed with a bluish-green sheen, with glossy bright blue on the throat and undertail.
facts.quote: It is dark brown but this is heavily washed with a bluish-green sheen on the back and wing coverts. Its belly and undertail coverts are light coloured, and it has glossy bright blue colouring on its throat and undertail.

facts.text: A mature dollarbird's short, wide bill is orange-red with a black tip.
facts.quote: Its bill is short and wide and in mature animals is coloured orange-red with a black tip.

facts.text: Females are slightly duller than males, but the two sexes look very similar overall.
facts.quote: The females are slightly duller than the males but overall the two are very similar.

facts.text: Immature dollarbirds lack the blue throat of adults and have dark blackish-grey to brown bills and feet.
facts.quote: Immature birds are much duller than the adults and do not have the blue colouring on their throats. They also have dark blackish-grey to brown bills and feet instead of the red of the adults.

facts.text: It usually perches upright on a bare high branch, catching flying insects and often returning to the same perch within seconds.
facts.quote: most commonly seen singly with a distinctive upright silhouette on a bare branch high in a tree, from which it hawks for flying insects, often returning to the same perch after a few seconds

facts.text: The subspecies breeding in northern and eastern Australia arrives around September and leaves in April, wintering in New Guinea and nearby islands.
facts.quote: the latter in northern and eastern Australia between the months of September and April and winters in New Guinea and nearby islands

facts.text: Dollarbirds prefer open wooded areas with hole-bearing trees where they can build their nests.
facts.quote: The birds prefer open wooded areas with hole-bearing trees to build nests in.

facts.text: The name dollarbird comes from the round bluish-white wing patch, said to resemble a silver dollar coin.
facts.quote: The name "dollarbird" is from the round bluish-white patch on the wing, visible in flight or when stretching its wings, "said to resemble a silver dollar" (coin).
